source: MAFF Svay Rieng Provincial Department of Agriculture / Polinuovo (Robolino) Program - Report: "Project for Supporting and Promoting New Local Initiatives" - Subject: "Corn Cultivation Techniques via Farmer-Led New Initiative" (បច្ចេកទេសដំដុៈដំណំពោតសអមផ្តូចផ្តើមថ្មីរបស្កសិករ), Ruessei Am village, Khsem commune, Kampong Ro district, Svay Rieng province
text:
Approximately 10 volunteer farmers in Ruessei Am village each ran their own small corn cultivation trial plot using broadly the same land-preparation and fertilizing method (see the accompanying methodology entry), but with minor individual variation in timing and fertilizer amounts, reflecting each farmer's own recorded practice. Growth was tracked weekly: across most farmers' plots, stalk height progressed from roughly 6 cm at week 1, to 9-12 cm at week 2, 11-15 cm at week 3, 14-18 cm at week 4, 23 cm at week 5, then a sharp jump to roughly 110-130 cm at week 6, and about 130 cm at week 7 (with a slight further increase in some plots up to 130-140 cm), while leaf count rose from about 2 leaves at week 1 to 15-18 leaves by week 6-7. A summary bar chart ("stalk height and leaf-count averages" chart) shows nearly all 10 farmers reaching close to the same final average stalk height (about 130 cm), with one farmer's plot (belonging to a farmer named "Nut Suong") standing out as visibly taller in the chart bar.

Harvest was done in three successive picking rounds per plot, generally starting about 80 days (some plots recorded 85 days) after planting. Individual plot totals recorded in the text tables ranged from about 72 to 80 kg of corn per trial plot across the farmers whose figures were fully legible (e.g. one farmer: 38 kg + 25 kg + 17 kg = 80 kg over 3 rounds; another: 38 kg + 24 kg + 10 kg = 72 kg). A separate summary bar chart of total yield per farmer (total yield in kg) shows most of the 10 farmers clustered in a similar range (roughly 72-90 kg total), with one farmer's plot yielding conspicuously more (visually well above 100 kg on the chart, consistent with the report's own conclusion naming that farmer as the top performer).

NOTE ON DATA QUALITY: several of the individual farmer result tables in the source PDF have blank or illegible numeric cells (missing digits for hole spacing, base fertilizer amount, planting date, and some week-by-week growth figures) — these gaps are in the source document itself and were not filled in or guessed. Also, harvest-to-planting duration is inconsistently recorded across plots (80 days for most, but 85 days for at least two plots), which may reflect real variation between farmers' plots rather than an error.

CONCLUSION (as stated in the report): despite the small scale and simple nature of each farmer's individual trial, the report concludes the exercise produced concrete, tangible results and was easy for farmers to carry out using their own techniques. It highlights the farmer named Nut Suong as achieving the highest yield among all participants, and recommends that other farmers replicate that farmer's fertilizer regimen, given as: base/bottom fertilizer of 0.2 kg per plot (applied before planting); first top-dressing application of 0.9 kg chemical fertilizer plus 10 kg organic fertilizer; second top-dressing application of 0.9 kg chemical fertilizer plus 10 kg organic fertilizer; and third top-dressing application of 0.9 kg chemical fertilizer plus 10 kg organic fertilizer. FLAGGED DISCREPANCY: these conclusion-page fertilizer figures (0.2 kg base, 0.9 kg chemical per top-dressing round) are notably smaller than the amounts shown earlier in this same farmer's own individual results table (base fertilizer ~0.5 kg, and top-dressing chemical fertilizer amounts of roughly 5, 8, and 11-12 kg per round with 9-21 kg of organic fertilizer per round). The source document does not reconcile this difference; it is reported here as-is rather than guessed at.
